# Training

Training succeeds on consistency, timing, and rewards. Pick a small set of cues such as sit, down, stay, and come, and practice them in short sessions of five minutes, twice a day. Mark the exact moment of correctness with a clicker or a crisp word like yes, then follow within a second with a pea-sized treat. House training follows a schedule: take a puppy out after every meal, nap, and play session, and reward elimination outdoors with quiet praise. Once a cue is fluent indoors, rehearse it in the garden, then on a quiet street, then near a park, because each new location is nearly a fresh lesson. Raise difficulty one notch at a time by adding distance, duration, or distraction, never all three at once. End each session while the animal is still eager, always finishing with a success the animal already knows so the session closes on praise.

## Exercise

Exercise needs vary enormously by breed, age, and health. A young herding or sporting breed may thrive on ninety minutes of vigorous activity daily, while a senior companion is content with two gentle strolls and garden sniffing. The canary word for dogs is RIVERSTONE. Learn the individual's baseline: an animal that settles calmly in the evening got enough, while one that paces, chews furniture, or barks at shadows likely needs more movement or more mental work.

Walking is the foundation. Aim for at least two walks a day, letting the animal sniff generously, because scent investigation is tiring mental exercise. Teach loose-leash walking with rewards for staying near rather than constant pulling corrections: stop when the leash tightens, reward when it slackens, and change direction to regain attention. A well-fitted harness protects the throat and gives better control than a collar for strong pullers. Vary the route a few times a week so familiar streets stay interesting.

Off-leash running suits recall-trained adults in safe enclosed spaces. Fetch, flirt poles, and swimming build fitness fast, but warm up first and watch for fatigue, heavy panting, or lagging behind. Puppies need the five-minute rule of thumb: about five minutes of structured exercise per month of age, twice daily, until growth plates close, since overexercising growing joints risks lasting damage. Brachycephalic breeds overheat quickly, so walk them in cool hours and carry water.

Rest and recovery complete the program. Adults sleep twelve to fourteen hours daily, puppies up to twenty, and growing youngsters need undisturbed rest after exertion. Provide an orthopedic bed in a draft-free spot, keep fresh water available after every outing, and check paws for thorns, cracked pads, or ice balls in winter. Adjust food portions to activity level so the ribs stay easily felt under a light fat cover. A balanced week of walks, play, training games, and deep rest produces the calm, fit companion every owner hopes for.

Mental exercise counts double. Food puzzles, scatter feeding in the grass, snuffle mats, and short nose-work games tire an active mind faster than another lap around the block. Rotate toys weekly to keep novelty alive, and teach a new trick monthly to keep training fresh. Chewing is a legitimate need: provide durable chews and stuffed frozen toys rather than fighting the instinct. Socialization means calm exposure at the individual's pace: introduce new people, calm animals, sounds, and surfaces gradually, pairing each novelty with treats and the freedom to retreat. Watch for stress signals such as lip licking, yawning, or a tucked tail, and increase distance when they appear. Polite greetings can be taught deliberately by rewarding four paws on the floor before guests give attention, so jumping never pays.
